questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Which side of the shared boundary owns a control
questions.learningObjective: Identify the party that should own a control at a shared boundary.
questions.stem: A shared service boundary has one control that neither the platform team nor the consuming team will accept, and the release keeps slipping. Which side should own this control?

options.text: The side that operates the component can enforce it where the decision is actually made.
The consuming team should own it, because the consumer experiences the damage when the control fails.
options.misconception: assumes the harmed party must implement the control

options.text: The platform team should own it, because a shared boundary implies one owner for every control on it.
options.misconception: believes one shared boundary means one owner for all controls

options.text: Neither side should own it, because shared boundaries work best when responsibility for each control stays ambiguous.
options.misconception: treats unclear ownership as a legitimate shared responsibility

questions.explanation: Ownership follows the component a control governs, so the side that operates it can enforce the control where the decision is made. Being the party harmed by a failure does not confer the ability to apply the control.
questions.hint: Ask who operates the component the control governs.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a sign-in record establishes
questions.learningObjective: State what a sign-in record proves and what it leaves unproven.
questions.stem: A sign-in record shows a successful authentication for an engineer from a managed laptop using a federated identity. Explain precisely what this record establishes and what it does not establish.

answer.exemplar: The record establishes that an authentication event completed for that named identity at that time, from that device, using the listed method, and that a session or token was issued. It does not establish that the person present was the account holder, that the device is uncompromised, that every action later taken under the session is authorised, or that the session cannot be revoked later.

questions.explanation: A sign-in record is evidence about an authentication event: which identity authenticated, when, from where and how. It is not evidence that the endpoint is trustworthy or that later actions were authorised.
questions.hint: Separate the authentication event from later authorisation.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The least privilege a service principal needs
questions.learningObjective: Choose which grants a least privilege review should remove first.
questions.stem: A service principal for a nightly export job holds 6 action grants on 3 resources. The review records 2 grants never used in 90 days, 1 grant used only for reads, and 1 grant needed only during the monthly close. Which grants should be removed first?

options.text: Remove the 2 unused grants and the monthly close grant, since both are proven unnecessary at 90 days of use.
options.misconception: treats infrequent but necessary grants as unnecessary

options.text: Remove only the read grant, because read access can always be replaced by a copy of the exported data.
options.misconception: assumes read access can be substituted by a cached copy

options.text: Remove the 2 unused grants, then add a broad write grant so the job can self-correct any missing export.
options.misconception: adds privilege to compensate for a missing grant

options.text: Remove the 2 unused grants and narrow the read grant, keeping the close-period grant time-scoped.

questions.explanation: Least privilege removes grants no workflow needs and narrows those still needed. The read grant can be reduced, the close grant is needed at close time, and adding write access widens the blast radius.
questions.hint: Usage frequency alone does not decide a grant's fate.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A role and a permission are not the same thing
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a role from the permissions it bundles.

stimulus.body: The billing service exposes three roles to application teams: reader, operator and administrator. A recent draft grants the operator role an ability to delete invoices, which the business team did not request. The platform lead argues the operator role must stay broad so that future duties are easy to add.

questions.stem: Given the brief, what is the correct relationship between the operator role and the ability to delete invoices, and how should the platform lead's argument be handled?

options.text: The operator role must include deletion so operators can finish invoice tasks without asking admins.
options.misconception: assumes convenience for operators justifies destructive permissions

options.text: Roles and permissions are the same, so the operator role covers everything the service knows.
options.misconception: confuses a role with the individual permissions it aggregates

options.text: Deletion should stay in the role but be hidden from the role definition, so users find it when needed.
options.misconception: believes hiding a permission in a definition equals not granting it

options.text: Deletion is a separate permission, and role breadth should come from new roles rather than pre-granting permissions.

questions.explanation: A role is a bundle of permissions, so removing deletion is a scope change rather than a contradiction. Future duties can be met by adding a role, and hiding a permission in a definition still grants it.
questions.hint: Think of a role as a named bundle of permissions.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The credential a managed identity removes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a managed identity removes and what it leaves unchanged.
questions.stem: First stage: a deployment pipeline needs a certificate to call a registry, and today it reads a long-lived password from a shared file. Second stage: the security review asks what a managed identity changes for that pipeline and what it leaves unchanged.

options.text: The pipeline stops storing secrets and also becomes exempt from any registry policy, because identity replaces policy.
options.misconception: assumes an identity replaces authorisation policy as well

options.text: The pipeline stops storing a secret to present, while its right to call the registry still depends on assigned roles.
The pipeline keeps the password but wraps it in a managed identity, so nothing about the stored value changes.
options.misconception: believes wrapping a stored password in an identity changes nothing

options.text: The pipeline no longer needs any identity at all, because the workload identity replaces every credential in use.
options.misconception: assumes a workload identity removes the need for identity

questions.explanation: A managed identity removes the secret the workload holds and proves. It grants no authority by itself: the call still needs a role and a policy that permit it.
questions.hint: Ask what the identity still needs in order to be allowed.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a short-lived credential bounds
questions.learningObjective: Identify precisely what a credential lifetime limits.
questions.stem: A design brief argues that replacing a year-long credential with one that expires in an hour settles the exposure question. What does the shorter lifetime actually bound?

options.text: It bounds both the lifetime of a stolen credential and the number of actions the credential can perform.
options.misconception: assumes a short lifetime also reduces authorised reach

options.text: It bounds the damage from a leaked credential only if the identity also holds no role at all.
options.misconception: confuses lifetime limits with permission scope limits

options.text: It bounds how long a stolen credential stays useful, not what that credential can reach while valid.
It bounds nothing on its own, because revocation already exists and makes lifetime irrelevant.
options.misconception: believes revocation makes credential lifetime irrelevant

questions.explanation: Expiry bounds the window in which a leaked credential can be replayed. It leaves the credential's reach untouched, since a valid short-lived token can still call every resource its role allows.
questions.hint: Ask how long a replayed credential remains useful.

questions.stem: A federation boundary delegates 12 authentication checks to an external identity provider and enforces 5 checks locally, for 17 checks in total. What fraction of the checks are enforced locally, expressed as a decimal to three places?

questions.hint: Divide local checks by the total number of checks.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Which side of the shared boundary owns a control
questions.learningObjective: Assign control ownership by the component each control governs.
questions.stem: A shared boundary hosts two controls: one about transport encryption and one about which records may be kept. Describe how to assign each control to an owner and justify the split.

answer.exemplar: Assign transport encryption to the side that terminates and operates the connection, since only that side can enforce the protocol and produce the evidence. Assign record retention to the side that owns the data and the legal obligation attached to it, because that is where the rule is applied and where a reviewer can see it working. Each owner then documents its control, tests it and reports results to the shared board.

questions.explanation: Controls should follow the component and the obligation they police, so each side keeps evidence for the part it can actually enforce. Encryption belongs with the connection operator and retention with the data owner.
questions.hint: Match each control to the party that can enforce it.

questions.learningObjective: Count distinct secret values held by an identity provider.
questions.stem: An identity provider directory holds 30 application registrations. Ten of them authenticate with a device-bound key and no central secret, and the remaining 20 each hold one shared secret. How many distinct secret values does the provider hold?

options.misconception: counts device-bound keys as centrally stored secrets

options.text: Ten values are held, because only the applications with keys contribute secrets.
options.misconception: picks the wrong group of applications to count

options.text: Twenty values are held, but the device-bound keys should be counted as a further ten.
options.misconception: double-counts the device-bound keys despite naming them

options.text: Twenty secret values are held, since the ten device-bound applications store nothing centrally.

questions.explanation: Only the 20 applications that hold a shared secret contribute to the total, so 20 values are held centrally. A device-bound key stays with the device, and counting it as a central secret would inflate the number by ten.
questions.hint: Count only the values the provider stores.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a sign-in record establishes
questions.learningObjective: Assess the evidentiary value of sign-in records and identify the missing field.

stimulus.body: During a review of quarterly access reports, an auditor found that the report only lists which identities signed in successfully. The auditor noted that the report cannot distinguish a shared workstation login from a personal device, and it omits any record of which role was active during the session.

questions.stem: Based on the note, what does a sign-in record establish about the session that follows it, and what additional field would most improve the report?

options.text: It shows the session had full administrative rights, so adding a field for administrator would help most.
options.misconception: assumes a successful sign-in implies administrative rights

options.text: It proves the person at the keyboard was the account owner, so a device identifier would close the gap.
options.misconception: treats a successful sign-in as proof of physical identity

options.text: It confirms nothing about identity, so the report should list only counts to avoid collecting detail.
options.misconception: believes collecting sign-in detail is inherently unsafe

options.text: It shows an identity authenticated at a time and method, and adding the role at sign-in would link each event to real authority.

questions.explanation: A sign-in record shows that an authentication event succeeded; it does not reveal what the session could do. Recording the role active at sign-in ties the event to the session's authority.
questions.hint: Think about what the session was allowed to do.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The least privilege a service principal needs
questions.learningObjective: Restructure a service principal grant to isolate a new capability.
questions.stem: First stage: a reporting service principal can read six tables and start two export jobs, and the business wants it to delete rows after a retention window. Second stage: how should the grant be restructured so the new capability is separated from the existing reads?

options.text: Add delete permission to the existing service principal role, since splitting it would complicate the deployment.
options.misconception: prefers convenience of one role over separating capabilities

options.text: Keep the read grants on the principal, add a separate deletion role, and give it only to the job that needs it.
Replace the existing role with one that includes reads, exports and deletion, then apply a time condition to it.
options.misconception: assumes a broad role plus a time condition equals least privilege

options.text: Keep the principal unchanged and let the retention job act through a human administrator account.
options.misconception: uses a human account so the service keeps no deletable grant

questions.explanation: A separate role keeps the read path unchanged and limits deletion to the workload that needs it. Adding deletion to the existing role, or wrapping a broad role in a time condition, widens exposure.
questions.hint: One capability, one role, one holder.

questions.topic: A role and a permission are not the same thing

questions.stem: A brief asks whether granting a service the ability to write to a queue makes it an administrator of that queue. Which statement correctly separates a role from a permission?

options.text: A role is a permission; writing to a queue promotes a service into the queue administrator role.
options.misconception: reverses the relationship, treating a role as a single capability

options.text: A role is the set of identities that hold a permission, so writing access defines who administers the queue.
options.misconception: confuses a role with the list of principals assigned to it

options.text: A role and a permission are identical, and any holder of write access is automatically an administrator.
options.misconception: assumes holding one permission confers the whole role

options.text: A role names a bundle of permissions; writing to a queue is one permission a role may contain.

questions.explanation: A role is a named bundle of permissions assigned to identities. Writing to a queue is one permission inside a bundle, so holding it neither confers the role nor its other permissions.
questions.hint: Think of a role as a named bundle of permissions.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a short-lived credential bounds
questions.learningObjective: Explain what changes and what does not when a credential lifetime is shortened.
questions.stem: A deployment currently uses a credential that never expires. Explain what changes if it is replaced with one that expires in fifteen minutes, and what does not change.

answer.exemplar: The window during which a leaked credential can be replayed falls from unlimited to fifteen minutes, and the blast radius of a compromise discovered later shrinks accordingly. What does not change is the reach of the credential while it is valid: it still carries the same role, the same permissions and the same trust relationship, so a short lifetime improves the odds of catching misuse but does not reduce the impact of misuse inside those fifteen minutes.

questions.explanation: Expiry shortens the replay window after a leak without touching the credential's reach. A short-lived credential can still perform every action its role allows for the whole of its validity window.
questions.hint: Separate how long it works from how much it can do.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a federation boundary actually delegates
questions.learningObjective: Determine the local check count after a delegation change.
questions.stem: A federated boundary delegates 24 checks to an external provider, of which 6 are identity checks and 18 are context checks. A proposal would take over the context checks, leaving only the identity checks delegated. How many checks would then be enforced locally?

options.text: The local count would rise to 6, because only the six identity checks would be delegated.
options.misconception: miscounts the delegated set and treats the identity checks as local

options.text: All 18 context checks would be enforced locally, so the local count rises from 0 to 18 of the 24 checks.
The local count would rise to 12, splitting the context checks evenly between the two sides.
options.misconception: assumes a proposal splits the context checks evenly

options.text: The local count would stay at 0, because the boundary would still delegate the entire check set.
options.misconception: assumes the proposal removes the boundary rather than shifting work

questions.explanation: Only the 6 identity checks remain delegated, so the other 18 checks move to the local side and the local count becomes 18. Nothing in the proposal splits the context checks, so a count of 12 has no basis.
questions.hint: Count what stays delegated, then take the remainder.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Which side of the shared boundary owns a control
questions.learningObjective: Move a control to the side that owns the component it governs.

stimulus.body: During a boundary review the platform team noted that its team owns the queue and the consumer team owns the data written into the queue. questions.stem: According to the note, which control should move to the consumer side, and what should the platform side keep?

options.text: Payload validation belongs to the consumer team, while the platform keeps queue availability and delivery.
Everything should move to the consumer team, because the consumer ultimately decides what is a valid message.
options.misconception: moves every control to the party furthest downstream

options.text: Everything should stay with the platform team, because the queue is the single shared component in the path.
options.misconception: assumes the shared component should own every control

options.text: The runbook should be left unchanged, since a shared error path avoids blame between the two teams.
options.misconception: prefers one blunt shared runbook over accurate ownership

questions.explanation: The control follows the thing it governs: payload shape is the consumer's responsibility, while delivery and availability belong to the queue operator. A shared runbook cannot fix misrouted escalation.
questions.hint: Match the control to the component it governs.

questions.topic: What an identity provider concentrates

questions.stem: First stage: a team runs 18 internal applications against one identity provider, and every application has its own client secret stored in the release pipeline. Second stage: the team proposes federating all 18 applications under one group credential to reduce secret handling. What does that proposal actually change?

options.text: It keeps 18 stored secrets but moves them into the identity provider's own vault.
options.misconception: assumes storing secrets elsewhere removes the duplication

options.text: It lets each application keep its own secret while letting them share one certificate for transport.
options.misconception: confuses grouping with transport certificates

It removes the need for client secrets entirely because federated apps authenticate with a token.
options.misconception: believes a group credential eliminates client secrets

questions.explanation: Grouping reduces the count of stored secrets but concentrates their blast radius: one leaked value now authenticates all 18 applications. Fewer secrets is not the same as less exposure.
questions.hint: Count the secrets and weigh the blast radius.

questions.topic: What a sign-in record establishes

options.misconception: reads the record as proof of presence and approval

options.text: That an identity authenticated at a stated time and source using a stated method, but not about intent.
That the device which authenticated was free of tampering and passed all hardening checks.

questions.explanation: A sign-in record is a statement about an authentication event: identity, time, source and method. Physical presence, device integrity and the safety of everything that follows are outside what it can support.
questions.hint: Ask only what the recorded fields actually assert.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A role and a permission are not the same thing
questions.learningObjective: Compare a predefined role grant with an explicit permission grant.
questions.stem: A brief describes granting a team the built-in contributor role on a storage container. Explain how that differs from granting the team the ability to read and upload specific files.

answer.exemplar: A built-in role hands over a fixed bundle of permissions chosen by whoever designed the role, so the team's reach is whatever that bundle contains, including anything added later to the role definition. Granting specific abilities such as read and upload gives the team exactly those two capabilities and nothing else, including no ability to delete, share or change permissions. The second form is easier to review because the granted set is visible in the assignment itself.

questions.explanation: A predefined role grants whatever its definition contains, which may grow over time, while an explicit permission grant grants only the listed actions. The second form keeps the team's reach visible at assignment time.
questions.hint: Compare the fixed bundle with the listed actions.

questions.stem: According to the note, what would a shorter credential lifetime have bounded, and what would it still have left untouched?

options.text: It would have prevented the token from being reusable at all, because a short token cannot be replayed.
options.misconception: assumes short-lived tokens cannot be replayed

options.text: It would have cut the exposure window and also removed the need for the weekly log review.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why authentication evidence does not prove authorisation.
questions.stem: A compliance reviewer asks whether the presence of a successful sign-in record for an administrator proves that the administrative change was authorised. Explain the reasoning and the missing evidence.

answer.exemplar: The sign-in record establishes only that an authentication event for that administrator identity succeeded at a stated time and place. It says nothing about the change itself, because authorisation for a specific action lives in the approval trail, the request ticket, the recorded justification and the policy decision, not in the authentication event. To conclude the change was authorised you would need those artefacts and the audit entries showing which identity performed the change under which role.

questions.explanation: Authentication proves who presented a credential, not that a particular action was permitted. Authorisation evidence lives in the approval record, the ticket and the policy, none of which a sign-in entry contains.
questions.hint: Authentication and authorisation are separate claims.

options.misconception: widens the existing role because the request comes from the same workload

options.text: Add deletion as a separate permission in a new role assigned narrowly, keeping the executor role at three permissions.

questions.topic: What a short-lived credential bounds
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a short lifetime alone does not make a call safe.
questions.stem: A brief claims that issuing a token that lives for five minutes makes a service-to-service call safe. Explain the part of that claim the lifetime can support and the part it cannot.

answer.exemplar: A five minute lifetime supports the claim only in the sense that a leaked or stolen token cannot be replayed for long after the compromise. It cannot make the call safe while the token is live: a token presented in that window carries the full authority of the identity that issued it, so it can call every resource the caller's role allows. The exposure is therefore proportional to the reach of the identity, and reducing reach requires narrowing grants or scoping the target resource.

questions.explanation: Short lifetime limits how long a leaked token can be reused; it does not limit what a live token may do. The remaining exposure is governed by the reach of the issuing identity.
questions.hint: Ask what a live token can still reach.

answer.exemplar: A sign-in record is good evidence that a particular identity authenticated at a particular time from a particular source, so it can place an account at an endpoint. It breaks down when the inference moves from the account to the person: shared accounts, shared kiosks, delegated sessions and stolen credentials all place the identity in the record without placing the intended user there. For evidential use the record must be joined with device and session data and the approval trail before it can carry an attribution claim.

questions.hint: Ask whether each grant is used and by which step.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A role and a permission are not the same thing
questions.learningObjective: Handle a role change request that conflicts with a policy.

stimulus.body: A policy states that the operations team shall hold the administrator role on the deployment platform, and that all other teams shall hold either the operator role or the viewer role. A recent request asks for the operations team to drop the administrator role because its members mostly deploy rather than administer.

questions.stem: Given the policy, how should the request be handled, and what does the request reveal about how roles and permissions are being treated?

options.text: Approve the request and drop the administrator role, since unused administrative rights need not be held.
options.misconception: treats the policy as optional when duties differ from its assumption

options.text: Refuse the request, because the policy grants the administrator role and no alternative may be substituted.
options.misconception: reads the policy as naming one role with no permitted alternative

options.text: Grant the operations team the operator role, since the policy separates roles by duty rather than seniority.
Grant the operations team both roles, so nothing is lost while the policy is reconsidered.
options.misconception: keeps a broad role while pretending the request has been met

questions.explanation: The policy allows a different role for a different duty, so operations can take the operator role while administrators keep theirs. The request treats roles and permissions as identical.
questions.hint: Check whether the policy names one role or a choice.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The credential a managed identity removes
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a managed identity replaces a stored client certificate.
questions.stem: First stage: a service principal currently presents a shared certificate to reach a partner API, and the certificate is renewed manually every year. Second stage: the team proposes a managed identity with a short-lived credential instead.

options.text: The workload stops presenting a certificate, and the partner no longer needs to validate any workload identity.
options.misconception: assumes removing client certificates removes the partner's validation duty

options.text: The workload stops presenting a certificate, and access now depends on a short-lived token bound to its identity.
The workload keeps the certificate but renews it automatically through the managed identity, so nothing else changes.
options.misconception: assumes the identity only automates renewal of the old credential

options.text: The workload keeps the certificate and the managed identity is added only to record who requested the renewal.
options.misconception: treats the managed identity as an attribution label

questions.explanation: A managed identity with a short-lived credential removes the stored certificate and replaces it with a token the workload obtains for itself. The partner must still validate it.
questions.hint: Ask what the partner still has to verify.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a short-lived credential bounds
questions.learningObjective: State precisely what a credential lifetime bounds.
questions.stem: A short-lived credential is described as bounding compromise. Which statement is the most precise account of what it bounds?

options.text: It bounds the time window in which a leaked credential can be used, leaving its reach unchanged while valid.
It bounds both the window of misuse and the number of resources the credential may address during it.
options.misconception: claims expiry reduces the authorised reach as well

options.text: It bounds the window of misuse only when the credential is also bound to a single named destination.
options.misconception: makes expiry conditional on destination binding

options.text: It bounds the window of misuse, provided revocation exists for the case where misuse is detected early.
options.misconception: makes expiry conditional on the existence of revocation

questions.explanation: Expiry is a pure time bound on reuse; the credential's reach while it is valid is set by its grants and is unaffected. Revocation and destination binding are separate controls.
questions.hint: Expiry limits time; grants limit reach.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a federation boundary actually delegates
questions.learningObjective: Compute the local share of checks after several checks move outward.
questions.stem: A federation boundary delegates 18 of its 24 sign-in checks to an external provider and enforces 6 locally. A redesign moves 3 of the local checks outward. What percentage of the 24 checks are then enforced locally?
questions.explanation: Moving 3 checks outward leaves 3 enforced locally out of 24 total checks, and 3 divided by 24 is one eighth. As a percentage that is 12.5, with the delegated count rising to 21.
questions.hint: Recount the local checks, then divide by the total.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Which side of the shared boundary owns a control
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a shared boundary needs a written ownership statement.
questions.stem: Explain why a shared boundary needs a written statement of which side owns each control, and what it prevents.

answer.exemplar: Without a written statement, ownership of a shared control is inferred from who complains loudest or who happened to build the component, and that inference changes whenever staff move. The statement removes the argument from the incident path by naming the owner of each control, the evidence they produce and who may grant exceptions. Its value is not that it settles every case but that any disagreement now has a document to point at, and controls that nobody owns become visible instead of silently unenforced.

questions.explanation: A written ownership statement removes inference from the incident path by naming the owner, the evidence and the exception authority for each control. It also exposes controls nobody has claimed.
questions.hint: It replaces argument with a named owner.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an identity provider concentrates
questions.learningObjective: Count distinct secret values held for grouped client registrations.
questions.stem: An identity provider directory lists 40 registered applications, 12 of which share one federated credential group, while the remaining 28 each hold their own secret. How many distinct secrets does the provider hold?

options.text: 40 minus the 12 grouped applications, giving 28 distinct secret values in total.
options.misconception: subtracts grouped applications instead of replacing their secrets with one

options.text: 40 applications each with a secret, giving 40 distinct values before any grouping is applied.
options.misconception: counts each application separately and ignores the grouping

options.text: 12 grouped applications sharing one secret plus 28 remaining, giving 13 distinct values overall.
options.misconception: divides the total by the group size instead of removing duplicates

options.text: 28 plus one shared secret for the group of 12, giving 29 distinct secret values in total.

questions.explanation: Each of the 28 ungrouped applications contributes its own secret, and the 12 grouped applications share one value between them, so 29 secrets are held. Counting all 40 separately overstates the total by eleven.
questions.hint: One shared value replaces twelve separate ones.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a sign-in record establishes
questions.learningObjective: Determine what sign-in records establish about a claimed approval.

stimulus.body: An engineer recalled that a colleague approved a change in a chat message, and the team wants to use the sign-in records of both accounts to prove the approval happened. The records show both accounts signed in successfully on the same day, and one of them has a record showing an administrative action.

questions.stem: According to the note, what do the sign-in records actually establish about the claimed approval, and what would be needed to establish it?

options.text: They establish that the approval happened, since both accounts were signed in when it was given.
options.misconception: treats simultaneous authentication as proof of a specific exchange

options.text: They show both accounts authenticated that day; proving the approval needs the approval artefact itself.
They establish that the senior account gave the approval, because an administrative action appears in its record.
options.misconception: reads an unrelated privileged action as evidence of approval

options.text: They establish nothing at all, because sign-in records can never be used as evidence in a review.
options.misconception: dismisses sign-in records as unusable evidence

questions.explanation: The records support only that the accounts authenticated on that day. Approval is a separate act with its own artefact, and an unrelated administrative action does not stand in for it.
questions.hint: Ask what artefact actually records the approval.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The least privilege a service principal needs
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether a principal is read-only and what an extra role adds.
questions.stem: First stage: a read-only service principal is granted read on one dataset plus a role that also grants read on three more datasets. Second stage: the owner asks whether the principal is genuinely read-only and what the extra role adds.

options.text: It is not read-only, because a role may quietly include write actions that the listing does not show.
options.misconception: assumes a role may contain write permissions not visible in its listing

options.text: It is read-only, and the extra role adds nothing because read access was already granted on the first dataset.
options.misconception: misses that the additional datasets are separate grants

options.text: It is read-only, and the extra role adds three read grants that can never be used together.
options.misconception: assumes separate read grants cannot be exercised together

options.text: It is read-only, and the extra role adds three more read grants, so removing it would cut the datasets from four to one.

questions.explanation: Every grant listed is a read, so the principal remains read-only. The extra role contributes three further read grants on other datasets, so dropping it reduces the reachable dataset count from four to one.
questions.hint: Check the actions in every grant, then count datasets.
